content.summary_of_the_paper:
The observation is made that (a) quantisation methods with a deterministic encoder (and possibly random decoder), and (b) quantisation methods with a (possibly infinite) source of shared randomness between encoder and decoder; are two ends of a spectrum, and that it is interesting to study intermediate methods where a limited quantity of randomness (say 1 to 3 bits) is shared between encoder and decoder.

A method called MultiQuan is proposed to efficiently communicate in this setting. Small scale experiments show that MultiQuan performs as expected, and can outperform methods with infinite shared randomness, due to the fact that the (lossless) encoder of the quantised index can specialise more easily in MultiQuan. Experiments on MNIST were also performed, and the results were again as expected.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
 - As far as I know (having read some, but not all of the relevant background literature), the work is novel.
 - The idea makes sense, and the mathematical analysis presented seems accurate.

### Weaknesses
 - I was not convinced by the motivation of the paper, or that it is sufficiently significant and within scope for ICLR. More specifically:
   - On MultiQuan itself, is the point primarily theoretical or is this method actually supposed to make it into production one day? If the latter, then is it too much to ask for the authors to demonstrate the advantages of the method over existing techniques on a realistic task? The MNIST experiments were the closest the paper came to this, but there was no discernible difference in image quality between MultiQuan and the pre-existing methods to which it was compared.
   - The paper worked within the 'Rate-Distortion-Perception' trade-off framework, introduced in Blau and Michaeli (2019). Unfortunately I have not read that work, but I was able to understand the idea from the introduction given in the paper under review. I'm not convinced that the 'Perception' is an important metric for lossy compression (the name 'perception function' also seems misleading, but that's a separate issue). I would be persuaded if I saw empirical evidence that optimising this quantity led to improvements over the existing best metrics (which all also claim to be 'perceptual').
   - The paper is focussed on a very specific sub-topic of lossy compression, and I'm not sure whether it is sufficiently relevant to the audience of ICLR, which is a machine learning conference. I would be interested to hear the views of the authors and other reviewers on this.
 - The paper contained _a lot_ of typos (see non-exhaustive list below).
 - I found Section 4.1 (one of the central technical sections of the paper) pretty difficult to follow, and I wonder if it could have been presented more clearly.
 - Related work should be discussed _in the main paper_, not in an appendix.

### Typos and minor questions/points
 - The term 'common randomness' should be defined early on, in the introduction, where it is first used.
 - Second paragraph on pg 2, "the dithering based approach will utilizes..." should be "the dithering based approach will utilize..."
 - Second paragraph of Section 4, "uncoutable" should be "uncountable"
 - The meaning of the first sentence of the last paragraph on page 6 was not clear to me, this is where I first got lost in this section.
 - Figure 4 looks unprofessional.
 - First bullet point of section 4.2, "optimal" should be "optimum".
 - First paragraph of section 5.2, "We follows" should be "We follow"; "MutliQuan" should be "MultiQuan"
 - Caption of figure 6, "respective" should be "respectively"
 - Halfway down page 9, "Kanotorovich" should be "Kantorovich". Just below that the citation to Gulrajani et al. should all be in parentheses.
 - In the title of Appendix D, "Optimzing" should be "Optimizing".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
Generally the writing was ok, and I was able to understand the paper. However, I thought that things could have been clearer, and expressed more concisely.

### Novelty
As far as I know the method is novel, however I am not an expert on this specific topic.

### Reproducibility
The authors say that they plan to release their code 'upon acceptance'. It might be possible to reproduce the experiments based only on the information in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: As I have mentioned above, I am not an expert on the particular topics of the 'Rate-Distortion-Perception' trade-off, or communication with shared randomness. However, my opinion is that the paper should not be accepted to ICLR, for the reasons outlined above under 'Weaknesses'.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies quantization schemes for the rate-distortion-perception framework. The paper begins by analyzing and comparing deterministic quantization and dithered quantization on the unit circle and showing the latter is essentially a combination of an infinite number of deterministic quantizer. It then proposes MultiQuan. The key idea is to use a set of N deterministic quantizers. MultiQuan is proven to approach the distortion of dithered quantization. Next, the paper extends MultiQuan to handle any symbol probability density and to enable trainable thresholds. Empirical experiments then compare the proposed MultiQuan to dithered quantizer and to deterministic quantization on MNIST using Wasserstein GAN as a deep compression architecture. MultiQuan is shown to outperform both baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
* Section 3 does a great job introducing dithered quantizers and the proposed approach. I think the authors did a good job explaining their approach.
* The gain over the baselines in the experiments seem significant. 

**Weaknesses**
* Compression experiments are only done on the MNIST data set. Even though the main contribution is theoretical, I was underwhelmed by the experiments and I think the paper would be stronger with experiments on real images. Likewise, the experiments are done using a Wasserstein GAN. Although used in previous similar work, I am not aware of state-of-the-art compression models using such an architecture. The relationships with auto-encoders optimizing the rate/distortion trade-off is not discussed. Finally, this work uses a Wasserstein GAN trained during the experiment as the metric for perception. Unless I missed it, the relationship between this GAN and perceptual metrics such as MS-SSIM is not covered in the paper either. This makes it difficult to assess the impact this paper could have. 
* Figure references should be checked. I think figure 4 are 5 are not discussed or referred to in the text. In addition, the text sometimes uses "Figure X" and sometimes "Fig.".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The paper is rather clear and well written.
   * I do not understand the notation under the min in the equation on p2.
* Imho, the reproducibility of the paper could be better. No code is provided.  The architecture of the networks is not described in the paper. The main paper mentions that the experiments are similar to Blau and Michaeli (2019)  while appendix E.2 states that the architecture is from Zhang et al. (2021). I found it a bit confusing.
* The contribution seems novel to me. 

Some typos:
* cases of with full (p2)
* and the finally (p3)
* f(x) instead of f_n(x) ? (p7)
content.summary_of_the_review: I would not recommend the paper for acceptance. The proposed idea is interesting and well explained, but to me the lack of experiments or discussion on the relationships between the proposed contribution and state-of-the-art in neural compression does not make it interesting enough.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides a novel approach to utilizing common randomness in rate-distortion-perception (RDP) coding by interpolating scalar quantization with deterministic encoder and dithered quantizer, under the condition of perfect perception. Quantization of uniform source on the unit circle is studied in detail, on the basis of which the MultiQuan procedure is proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
1. Overall the paper has been written very clearly.
2. The proposal is interesting and seems novel, as far as I can tell.
3. A thorough analysis was made on the unit-circle setting with perfect perception, as summarized in Theorems 3.1-3.3.
### Weaknesses
1. Practical significance of the proposal is questionable, as only a toy example of compressing MNIST images is provided as a real-world problem.
2. As for the image compression experiment in Section 5.2:
   1. Although the proposal is compared against the deterministic encoder and the dithered quantizer, there is no comparison with any other approach to RDP coding.
   2. It seems that how the authors evaluated $F_X$ and its inverse is not described.
   3. According to Appendix E.2, "encoding with uniform thresholds" was employed in the experiment, so that we cannot see how efficient the threshold optimization methods proposed in Section 4.2 are.
3. I wonder whether it is possible to extend the proposed framework from scalar quantization to vector quantization of a few (not many) samples. There seems no argument provided on such possible extension.

### Minor points:
- Page 1, line 6: one (at) a time
- Page 2, line 7: will utilize(s)
- Page 2, line 19: two extreme cases (of) with
- Page 2, line 42: referred to (as)
- Page 4, Figure 1 (c): 7 out of 9 figures seem incorrect. From (4), the quantizer outputs 1 when $\theta(x)\in[-Z,\pi-Z)\mod2\pi$, but these figures seem to assume, incorrectly, that it outputs 1 when $\theta(x)\in[Z-\pi,Z)\mod2\pi$. The locations of the dots representing the reconstruction also seem to be imprecise.
- Page 4, line 21: Extra space after "Fig. 1 (c)".
- Page 5, line 10: which uniformly partition(s)
- Page 5, line 11: by offset(t)ing
- Page 5, line 33: Theorem(s) 3.1-3.3
- Page 7, line 7: Is "$f(x)$ and $n$" $f_n(x)$?
- Page 7, line 28: that update(s) the thresholds
- Page 8, Figure 5: In both cases one can see that in a certain range of bitrate "private randomness only" seems to outperform "dithered quantization". I would appreciate a possible explanation to this.
- Page 8, line 16: Figure 7 $\to$ 5
- Page 8, line 28: We follow(s)
- Page 8, line 32: Mu(tl$\to$lt)iQuan
- Page 9, line 11: Kan(o)torovich's

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies quantizers under a rate-distortion-perception (RDP) principle and explores how the amount of shared randomness affects rate-distortion functions. The paper mainly considers the scenario of perfect perception, i.e., the law of reconstructed data exactly matches that of the original data. 

Subject to perfect perception, the authors propose a quantizer MultiQuan and characterize its distortion function as a function of quantization level (L) and amount of shared randomness (N) for the special case where the data is uniformly distributed over a (2-dim) circle. In addition, the optimal rate-distortion function (assuming an infinite amount of shared randomness) is specified for the 2-d circle case. These results generalize the previous result in [Theis et al., 2021]. 

Next, the authors extend this idea to general offset quantizers and show how to achieve perfect perception when the distribution of original data is known. Finally, empirical results for synthetic distributional data and neural network-based compression data are given.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I like Theorem 3.2 and 3.3 a lot since they not only characterize the achievable results but also give lower bounds on the rate-distortion functions and hence complement previous results of [Theis et al., 2021]. Also, I like the one-shot setting considered in this paper because it does not require a large sample size (which may not be true in practice). In addition to neural image compression, I think the proposed quantization/compression scheme can potentially be used in federated learning or analytics.

Weaknesses

- The MultiQuan scheme considered in Section 3 seems to be only a small modification of [Theis et al., 2021]. In addition, I find Theorem 3.1-3.3 very restricted as they only apply to 2-d unit-circle. I think it is fine to use a simple example to illustrate the idea, but I would expect more general results after. For example, can the results be generalized when the data is uniformly distributed over a unit d-dim sphere?

- One of the main focuses of this paper is how the amount of shared randomness affects the rate-distortion function, but I find this part is somewhat underexplored, especially from the lower bound perspective. In particular, the optimal achievable rate-distortion region in Theorem 3.2 and 3.3 does not depend on N and can only be achieved when N is infinity, so it is unclear whether MultiQuan is optimal or not for finite N, even for the restricted 2-d unit circle example. Is it possible to characterize the general achievable region as a function of N?

- Though in this paper, the dithered encoder over the unit circle is attributed to [Theis and Agustsson, 2021], the same technique has been used frequently in differential privacy literature, albeit under a slightly different form and motivation. For example, the privatization mechanism PrivUnit proposed in [DJW16] induces uniform distributions over a d-dim (half-)sphere (Figure 4 in Section 4.2.3). This mechanism is then shown to be compressible to 1 bit in [EFMRSTT20] (see Section VI of [EFMRSTT20]), and the resulting compression mechanism is the same as the dithered encoder proposed in [Theis et al., 2021]. Note that [EFMRSTT20] considers the general d-dim setting, and later in [FT21], they show how to reduce the amount of shared randomness using a pseudo-random generator.

The resulting algorithms from these works seem to be very close to, if not the same as, what is proposed in this paper, and hence should be properly discussed.

[DJW16] Minimax Optimal Procedures for Locally Private Estimation
[EFMRSTT20] Encode, Shuffle, Analyze Privacy Revisited: Formalizations and Empirical Evaluation
[FT21] Lossless Compression of Efficient Private Local Randomizers
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation of this paper is good and easy to follow. This work mainly builds and improves upon [Theis and Agustsson 2021], and though it has some original ideas, I find the novelty and contribution are somewhat limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, though I like the problems and setups considered in this paper, I find the novelty is somewhat limited. Also, similar techniques that appear in the privacy literature should be properly discussed.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
